We want to understand what you meant by "I’m not certain if that specific placement aligns with our current internal guidelines just yet", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The positioning of the Order Summary block at the top of the page layout.
B) The vertical stacking order of the Payment Details section relative to the final action buttons.
C) The grouping of specific line items (like "Shipping" and "Total") within the summary box.

turns.a: I think it's probably closer to A, just in the sense that I was looking at how the overall flow of the page is structured. From a project standpoint, I’m always trying to keep an eye on whether we’re following established patterns for these types of flows. Since the Order Summary is positioned so prominently at the top, it's something I'd want to double-check against our standard requirements before we move too far into development.

turns.q: What specific information were you trying to verify or confirm when your eyes landed on the Order Summary block at the top?
turns.a: I think I was mainly looking to see if that section was intended to be a static confirmation or if it's meant to interact with the user in some way during this stage. From a project management perspective, I’m always trying to keep an eye on whether we are following established patterns for these types of flows, and I wasn't entirely sure if the prominence of that top block was just for clarity or if there were specific functional requirements tied to it. It's probably something the team would need to clarify before we finalize the handoff.

turns.q: If that section functioned exactly as you expected it to, what specific information would be most clear or prominent for you?
turns.a: I think it's probably the final total and the individual item prices, since those are currently the most visually heavy elements in that top block. From a project standpoint, I’d want to make sure that the user can clearly see what they are committing to before they reach the bottom of the page. If those figures were consistent in their styling, it might help keep the focus on the transaction details rather than any one specific item standing out more than the others.

turns.q: What specific visual elements or inconsistencies in the Order Summary layout currently prevent those figures from feeling like a cohesive, unified transaction summary?
turns.a: I think it's probably the way the typography is handled for the different items, specifically how much larger and bolder the "Wireless Mouse" price is compared to the "Ergonomic Chair." Because that one figure stands out so much more than the others, it creates a bit of a visual imbalance. From a project standpoint, I'd want those figures to feel like they belong together as part of one summary, rather than having one item seem significantly more prominent than the other.

turns.q: When you first looked at this wireframe, what specific aspect of the layout or visual hierarchy were you evaluating when that imbalance in the Order Summary caught your eye?
turns.a: I think it was probably the way the "Order Summary" functions as a primary visual anchor right at the top of the page. From a project standpoint, I’m always trying to keep an eye on whether we are following established patterns for these types of flows, and because that section is so prominent, any inconsistency in how the items are presented—like the difference in font weight between the two products—could potentially lead to some confusion about what information is actually being highlighted.
